walkthroughs.body_html: Price level on y-axis, real GDP on x-axis. AD slopes down (price level up → real spending down). AS slopes up. Equilibrium where they cross. A rightward AD shift raises price level AND GDP — useful for inflation/growth analysis.
Fiscal: Treasury changes tax/spending — direct but slow. Monetary: Bank of England moves interest rates — fast but blunt. In a recession, expansionary fiscal (more G) + lower rates both boost AD.
Always evaluate: time lags, side-effects (e.g. inflation), magnitude (depends on multiplier), conflicts between objectives (growth vs inflation). Use 'however', 'depends on', 'in the long run'.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of EXPANSIONARY monetary policy?
options: Raising income tax
Cutting the Bank Rate
Selling government bonds
Reducing welfare spending

mcqs.q: Rising government borrowing pushes interest rates up, reducing private investment. This effect is called?
options: Multiplier
Crowding out
Inflation
Stagflation
A sustained rise in the general price level over time — reducing the purchasing power of money. Measured by the percentage change in a price index.
Inflation is when prices are high.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.

mcqs.q: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.
PED measures how flexible or stretchy a product is.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price — the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.
Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.
